title: Rules of thumb for option prices
objectives: Estimate an at-the-money option as about 0.4σ√T times the spot, and check it against Black-Scholes.
Say where the 0.4 comes from and where the rule fails

screens.title: Price against volatility
screens.prose: Interviewer: a one-year at-the-money option on a £100 share at 20% vol, no rates. What is it worth, without a calculator? First see how the price moves. Slide the time left.

state.caption: Call, S = K = £100, r = 0. Value against volatility.

screens.question: At $T = 1$ the vol doubles from 20% to 40%. What does the price do?

options.why: You squared the change, as variance does. At the money the price is close to a straight line in volatility.
You treated the price as fixed. At the money the call is all time value, so it is the most sensitive to volatility.

feedback.correct: At the money, price is nearly proportional to volatility.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the curve at 20% and at 40%.

explain.text: The curve is close to a straight line through zero. Doubling σ takes £7.97 to £15.85, a ratio of 1.99.

screens.title: A quarter of the time
screens.prose: Same option, same 20% vol. With a year left it is worth £7.97. Predict its price with three months left.

state.caption: Call, S = K = £100, r = 0. Value against volatility.

screens.question: What is the price with $T = 0.25$?

widget.label: Price in pounds
widget.accept: about £4.00: the price halves when time quarters

hints.text: Time falls by a factor of four. How did a doubling of vol change the price?
Time enters through its square root.
$\sqrt{0.25} = 0.5$, so the price halves: $7.97 \div 2 \approx 4.00$.

feedback.correct: Time quarters and the price halves: about £4.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the price at one year and at three months at 20%.

byKey.quarter: You divided by four, as if price fell in step with time. It falls with the square root of time.
byKey.same: You kept the one-year price. Less time means less room to move, so the call is cheaper.

explain.text: The three-month price is £3.99, a ratio of 0.5006: time quarters, price halves. Price grows with the square root of time, as the spread of a random walk does.

screens.title: Name the rule
screens.prose: Doubling $\sigma$ doubles the price and quartering $T$ halves it, so price follows $\sigma\sqrt T\,S$. For $S = £100$, $\sigma = 20\%$, $T = 1$, the constant is $7.9656 \div (0.2 \times 100) = 0.398$, about 0.4. That is the rule $C \approx 0.4\,\sigma\sqrt T\,S$, which gives £8.00 here against Black-Scholes £7.9656. Now use it on a £50 share at 32% vol with three months left.
screens.question: What does the rule give for the price?

hints.text: Put the three numbers into the rule.
Use $\sqrt{0.25} = 0.5$ and $\sigma = 0.32$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply 0.4, the vol, the square root of time and the spot.

byKey.no-root: You used $T$ where the rule needs $\sqrt T$. Three months is 0.5 of a year in the root.
byKey.whole-number-vol: You typed 32 for the vol. The rule needs 0.32.

explain.text: $0.4 \times 0.32 \times 0.5 \times 50 = 3.20$. Black-Scholes gives £3.19, so the rule is about 0.4% high.

screens.title: Where 0.4 comes from
screens.prose: At $r = 0$ and $K = S$, put the lines in order. $Z$ is a standard normal and $\varphi$ its density.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: The call is worth $E[\max(S_T - S, 0)]$, as the share is a martingale at $r = 0$. Here $S_T - S$ is about normal with spread $\sigma\sqrt T\,S$
Write $S_T - S = \sigma\sqrt T\,S\,Z$, so the call is $\sigma\sqrt T\,S\,E[\max(Z, 0)]$, because a constant comes out of an expectation
$E[\max(Z, 0)] = \int_0^\infty z\,\varphi(z)\,dz = 1/\sqrt{2\pi} = 0.3989$, because $-\varphi$ is an antiderivative of $z\varphi$
So $C \approx 0.3989\,\sigma\sqrt T\,S$, with nothing to discount at $r = 0$, and we round to $0.4\,\sigma\sqrt T\,S$
The mean of $\max(Z, 0)$ is 0.5, since $Z$ is positive half the time
lines.why: You gave the chance $P(Z > 0)$. The mean of $\max(Z, 0)$ weights each positive value by its size, and it is 0.3989.

hints.text: Start from what the call pays at expiry.
Scale out the spread before you take the expectation.
Payoff, scale, integral, then round.

feedback.correct: The 0.4 is the mean of a half-normal, $1/\sqrt{2\pi}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the payoff, scale it, integrate, then round.

byKey.x: You used the chance of a positive value. The rule needs the mean of the positive part, 0.3989.
byKey.c: The integral needs the scaled form from the line before it.

explain.text: The price is the average positive part of a normal with spread $\sigma\sqrt T\,S$. That average is $0.3989$ times the spread, which we round to 0.4.

screens.title: A straight line in vol
screens.prose: The rule is a straight line in $\sigma$, with slope $0.4\sqrt T\,S = 40$ per 1.00 of vol, or £0.40 a vol point. So vega is about price $\div\ \sigma$: 39.83 against the true 39.695. The vol now rises from 20% to 22%, with $T = 1$ and $S = 100$.

state.caption: Call, S = K = £100, r = 0. Value against volatility.

screens.question: How much does the call gain?

hints.text: Multiply the slope by the change in vol.
The change is 0.02 in the units the slope uses.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slope times the change in vol, as a decimal.

byKey.percent-slip: You used 2 as the change. The slope is per 1.00 of vol, so the change is 0.02.
byKey.half: You priced one vol point, £0.40. The vol rose by two.

explain.text: Slope times change is $40 \times 0.02 = 0.80$. Black-Scholes gives £0.7935: £8.7591 less £7.9656.

screens.title: Rates break the rule
screens.prose: Interviewer: same share, same 20% vol, one year, but rates are now 5%. Your rule still says £8.00. The model price is £10.45.
screens.question: Why does the rule fail here?

options.text: The strike's present value is £95.12, so the call is already £4.88 in the money in today's money. The rule prices only time value
Volatility should be entered in per cent
options.why: You blamed the units. The rule used 0.20 and was right at $r = 0$.

options.text: The quote includes a dealer margin
options.why: You assumed the quote is padded. £10.45 is the model value, with no margin.
You moved the vol. It is still 20%. The strike's present value is what changed.

hints.text: What changes between $r = 0$ and $r = 5\%$?
You pay the strike at expiry, so today it is worth less.
$100 e^{-0.05} = 95.12$, so the call is £4.88 in the money today.

feedback.correct: The rule priced time value only. Rates add the discounted strike gap.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the spot with the strike's present value.

byKey.units: You blamed the units. Nothing changed in how vol is written.
byKey.margin: You assumed a margin. The model value is £10.45 exactly.
byKey.rv: You moved the vol. Rates changed the strike's present value, not the vol.

explain.text: At $\sigma \to 0$ the call is worth $S - Ke^{-rT} = £4.88$, the in-the-money gap in today's money. The rule has no such term, so at 20% it misses by £2.45, half the gap.

screens.title: Add half the gap
screens.prose: Fix the rule by adding half of the present-value gap: $C \approx 0.4\,\sigma\sqrt T\,S + \tfrac12(S - Ke^{-rT})$. At $r = 5\%$ the gap is £4.88.
screens.question: What does the corrected rule give for the one-year call at 20%?

hints.text: Halve the gap before adding it to £8.00.
Half of £4.88 is £2.44.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add £8.00 to half of £4.88.

byKey.whole-gap: You added the whole £4.88. The rule needs only half of it.

explain.text: Discount the forward version, $e^{-rT}\left[0.4\sigma\sqrt T F + \tfrac12(F - K)\right]$ with $F = Se^{rT}$, and you get $0.4\sigma\sqrt T S + \tfrac12(S - Ke^{-rT})$. Here that is £10.44 against £10.4506.

screens.title: Away from the money
screens.prose: Edge case. Back to $r = 0$. The rule says £8.00 whatever the strike. Now move the strike away from the money.

state.caption: Call, S = £100, σ = 20%, T = 1, r = 0, against the strike.

screens.question: Read the curve: what is the call struck at 110, 10% out of the money, worth?

hints.text: Find the dashed line at 110 and read across to the axis.
The curve at 110 sits well below £8.
The value is about £4.29.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the height of the curve at a strike of 110.

byKey.rule: You read the rule's £8.00. The curve is the real price, and it has fallen a long way by 110.
byKey.atm: You read the at-the-money price. The strike is 110, so read the curve there.

explain.text: Out of the money by 5%, 10% and 20% the call is worth £5.91, £4.29 and £2.15. The rule says £8.00 each time and overstates by about a factor of two at 10%. It is for the money only.

screens.title: A client's straddle
screens.prose: Interviewer: a client asks for a one-month at-the-money straddle on a £120 share at 25% vol, rates zero. About 90 seconds. Give the reason, then the number. The call and put are worth the same.
screens.question: What is the straddle worth?

hints.text: The call and put are equal, so double one leg.
One leg is $0.4\sigma\sqrt T\,S$ with $\sqrt{1/12} = 0.2887$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price one leg with the rule, then double it.

byKey.one-leg: You priced one leg. A straddle is the call and the put.
byKey.no-root: You used $T = 1/12$ in place of its root, 0.2887.

explain.text: The straddle is $0.8\,\sigma\sqrt T\,S = £6.93$, against Black-Scholes £6.9084. As a share of the spot that is 5.77% (5.76% exact), the move needed to break even. Say aloud: about 0.8 of the vol over the root of time, times spot.

screens.title: The rule against the formula
screens.prose: Interviewer: show me how good the rule is. Write the rule, the exact at-the-money price with $r = 0$, and the rule's relative error. Use `math.erf`.
screens.question: Complete `atm_rule`, `bs_atm` and `rule_error`.

widget.starter:
from math import erf, sqrt

def atm_rule(S, sigma, T):
    """Rule of thumb: 0.4 * sigma * sqrt(T) * S."""
    ...

def bs_atm(S, sigma, T):
    """Black-Scholes at the money, r = 0: S * (2 * Phi(sigma * sqrt(T) / 2) - 1)."""
    # Phi(z) = 0.5 * (1 + erf(z / sqrt(2)))
    ...

def rule_error(S, sigma, T):
    """The rule divided by the exact price, minus 1."""
    ...
widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests on the three functions, compared with `math.isclose` to six places.

hints.text: Each function is one line of arithmetic.
`bs_atm` needs the normal cdf from `erf`: $\Phi(z) = \tfrac12(1 + \mathrm{erf}(z/\sqrt2))$.
`rule_error` is `atm_rule(...) / bs_atm(...) - 1`.

feedback.correct: The rule is within half a per cent of Black-Scholes at the money.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check `sqrt(T)` and the argument of the cdf, $\sigma\sqrt T/2$.

explain.text: The exact price is $S(2\Phi(\sigma\sqrt T/2) - 1)$, and the 0.4 is that with $\Phi$ replaced by its slope at 0. The error is about 0.4% across all three cases, and it grows as $\sigma\sqrt T$ does.

ideas: At the money with $r = 0$, a call is worth about $0.4\,\sigma\sqrt T\,S$: proportional to vol, to $\sqrt T$ and to the spot.
The 0.4 is $1/\sqrt{2\pi}$, the mean of a standard normal's positive part. Vega is about price divided by $\sigma$.
With rates add half of $S - Ke^{-rT}$, and away from the money do not use the rule at all.

formula.name: At-the-money rule
formula.note: At the money, r = 0; add half of S minus the discounted strike when r is not 0.

quiz.prose: At the money, r = 0, rule of thumb.
quiz.question: Select all that apply: which changes about double the price?

options.text: Doubling the spot and the strike together

options.why: You doubled the price for doubled time. Price goes with $\sqrt T$, so doubling $T$ gives about 1.41 times.

options.text: Doubling the spot at a fixed strike
options.why: You doubled only the spot. The option leaves the money and is worth about 12.6 times as much.

feedback.correct: Scale, vol and the square root of time all enter as products.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price is about $0.4\,\sigma\sqrt T\,S$ while the option stays at the money.

byKey.s2: A fixed strike means the option is no longer at the money.

explain.text: Price scales as $S$, $\sigma$ and $\sqrt T$. So doubling $S$ with $K$, doubling $\sigma$ and quadrupling $T$ each give about 1.99 to 2 times the price.
